title: Where Invitations Come From
subtitle: Member Personas · Invitation Source Breakout Sessions
howToUse: Each persona represents a real situation that exists at your club right now. During the breakout session, your group will read the story together, identify the exact moment the invitation pathway broke down, and discuss what specific behaviors would have changed the outcome.
These are not hypothetical. They are happening today — at every club, every month. The question is simply whether we recognize the moment before it passes.
"The future of this Club is shaped one thoughtful invitation at a time."
mission: Read the persona together — this person belongs to your club right now
Identify the exact moment the invitation pathway broke down
Discuss what specific behaviors would have changed the outcome
Prepare one key insight to share with the full room

personas.title: The Excited Joiner
personas.hook: Your fastest invitation source is sitting right in front of you.
personas.pull: We are creating members — but not creating sponsors.
story: Full Privilege. Matt and Erin Collins (38 and 36) joined the Club 45 days ago after receiving a personal invitation from friends they met through their children's school. Matt works in medical sales and Erin recently started her own interior design business. They have two children, ages 8 and 11.

The Collins family has quickly become active around the Club. Their kids attended junior golf clinics and swim team evaluations, and the family has already attended two social events and several dinners. Erin has posted photos from the Club on social media multiple times and has mentioned to staff how excited she is to finally 'have a place where everybody hangs out.'

During dinner one evening, Erin mentioned to a server that several families in their neighborhood had been asking questions about the Club after seeing her social media posts. The server smiled and replied, 'That's awesome!' — before walking away to another table.

The Collins family has now settled into a comfortable routine at the Club. They continue using the facilities regularly and often wave to familiar faces — but no one has discussed extending an invitation to their friends, explained how the sponsorship process works, or helped them think about who in their lives deserves to belong here.
personas.question: At what exact point did the new member pathway break down — and what behavior would have prevented it?

personas.title: The Social Regular
personas.hook: Our events are packed every month — but are they actually creating invitations?
story: Social Membership. Kelly and Jason Turner (44 and 46) have been members of the Club for nearly three years. They are highly social, know a large number of members, and rarely miss major Club events. Jason owns a local insurance agency while Kelly works part-time in event planning. Their children are older teenagers and no longer participate heavily in Club activities, allowing the couple to spend more time socially at the Club.

The Turners are often described as 'fun members.' They attend wine dinners, holiday parties, live music nights, and couples golf events regularly. Staff members know them well, and they frequently post pictures from events on social media. Several non-member friends often comment online about how much fun the Club appears to be.
At a recent summer concert event, Kelly mentioned to another member: 'We had three other couples ask if they could come tonight, but honestly we weren't sure if we were supposed to invite people.'

Meanwhile, the event itself was extremely successful from an attendance standpoint. The room was full, members stayed late, and food and beverage sales exceeded expectations. The following Monday, the management team celebrated the strong turnout during their department meeting.

No one discussed how many guests attended. No one noted whether guest information was collected. No one identified which members consistently bring friends who haven't yet been invited. No one followed up on a single potential invitation opportunity from the evening.

The Turners continue attending events regularly and still talk positively about the Club within their social circles — but the invitations that could naturally come from those conversations never happen.
personas.question: What would have turned this event into an invitation-producing experience — and what behaviors ensure events naturally become pathways to belonging?

personas.title: The One-Time Guest
personas.hook: Your members are already bringing future members to the Club. The question is whether your team recognizes them.
personas.pull: A hosted friend is not just a tee time. It is a live experience of belonging.
story: Full Privilege Guest Experience. Ryan Mitchell (42) was invited to play golf at the Club by his longtime friend and current member, Adam Pierce. Ryan owns a successful HVAC company and has lived in the area for over 10 years. He currently plays public golf courses with friends and clients but has casually discussed joining a private club several times over the years.

Adam coordinated the round directly with the golf shop and mentioned to the Golf Professional that Ryan had been asking questions about membership recently. The golf shop staff checked Ryan in politely, but beyond that the day operated like any normal guest round.

Ryan enjoyed the experience tremendously. The course conditions were excellent, service was friendly, and he especially enjoyed lunch afterward on the patio. During lunch, Ryan asked Adam several questions: 'How often do you use this place?' 'Are there a lot of younger members?' 'Is it hard to join?'
Adam answered casually but admitted he did not fully understand current membership options or how to extend a formal invitation.
Before leaving, Ryan thanked the staff and mentioned: 'This is honestly way more fun than fighting public tee times every weekend.'
The Membership Enrollment Director was never notified a guest was on property. No department head introduced themselves. No follow-up call or note was made afterward.
Two months later, Ryan joined another club closer to his office — after receiving a personal invitation from a member there.
personas.question: What behaviors would have turned this guest experience into the beginning of a membership journey?

personas.title: The Forgotten Advocate
personas.hook: Sponsors don't usually stop loving the Club — they stop feeling like it matters.
story: Full Privilege. Greg Anderson (61) has been a member of the Club for over 15 years and is widely respected throughout the membership. Over the years, Greg has personally extended invitations to five members, including two families who remain highly active today. He frequently hosted friends during his earlier years at the Club and was known for proudly introducing business associates and neighbors to the community he loved.

In recent years, Greg's involvement has become quieter. He still plays golf weekly and attends occasional dining events with his wife, but he no longer hosts friends as often as he once did. Several newer members know Greg casually but are completely unaware of his history and the role he played in building this Club's community.

At a recent dinner, Greg joked with another longtime member: 'I used to feel like they rolled out the red carpet when you brought someone out here.' He laughed while saying it — but later admitted he no longer really knows whether the Club even wants more members, how the invitation process works today, or whether the invitations he extended years ago are still remembered and valued.

Over time, the recognition of sponsors quietly disappeared. Celebrations became less frequent, staff turnover meant fewer people knew the history, and the culture of honoring those who helped build the membership faded without anyone deciding to let it go.
Greg still loves the Club deeply. He simply stopped feeling connected to the invitation process — because no one ever brought him back into it.
personas.question: What caused this member to stop extending invitations — and what behaviors would reignite his role as an advocate?

personas.title: The Connected Neighbor Who Was Never Connected
personas.hook: Communities grow one relationship at a time. So do membership pathways.
story: Athletic Membership Prospect. Emily and Trevor Reynolds (37 and 39) moved into a nearby neighborhood six months ago after relocating for Trevor's job in healthcare administration. They have two children, ages 7 and 10, who are heavily involved in swimming and tennis. Their Realtor mentioned the Club several times during the home buying process and described it as 'the center of the community.'

Since moving in, the Reynolds family has noticed the Club everywhere — families at the pool during summer, neighbors discussing events, social media posts from local members, busy tennis courts on weekends. Emily has expressed genuine interest in finding ways to meet people and build a life in their new community.

One evening at a neighborhood gathering, several residents joked: 'Everybody eventually ends up joining.' Emily later asked a neighbor: 'How do people even get invited?' The neighbor gave a vague answer and suggested she talk to somebody at the Club.
The Reynolds family has never received outreach from the Club, attended a Club event, met an Ambassador, or been formally welcomed into even a conversation about membership.
Meanwhile, they have already joined a nearby fitness facility and enrolled their children in local sports leagues. Routines are forming. Friendships are being built — somewhere else.
personas.question: What behaviors would have made this family feel welcome and expected before they built their life somewhere else?

personas.title: The Half-Connected Member
personas.hook: Upgrade opportunities are rarely hidden. Most clubs simply aren't looking for them.
story: Athletic Membership. Michelle Carter (48) joined the Club two years ago primarily for fitness classes, tennis, and social events. Since joining, she has become extremely comfortable at the Club and now visits four to five days each week. She frequently attends ladies social events, uses the dining room for lunches with friends, and has developed strong relationships with several Full Privilege members.

Michelle's husband, David, recently started joining her occasionally for dinner and has begun expressing interest in golf after spending time around other members. During a recent couples dinner, several friends encouraged the Carters to participate in an upcoming golf event.
Michelle laughed and replied: 'Oh we're not golf members — I wouldn't even know how that works.'

Over the last year, the Carters have attended multiple golf-adjacent events, brought guests to social functions, increased their overall Club usage significantly, and built close friendships with highly active Full Privilege members. Every signal is there.

Despite this, no one from the Club has had a natural conversation about what Full Privilege membership would look like for the Carters — not a sales conversation, simply an honest one between people who care about their experience here.
The Carters still enjoy the Club. They just don't know there is more waiting for them.
personas.question: At what point should the Club have recognized this family's readiness — and what would a natural, unhurried upgrade conversation look like?
